front: Why can Black-76 not price a rates option when the forward rate is negative, and what does Bachelier change?
back:
Black-76 assumes lognormal dynamics \(dF=\sigma_B F\,dW\), so \(F>0\) is built into the model. The \(\ln(F/K)\) term in \(d_1,d_2\) is undefined for \(F\le 0\) or \(K\le 0\).
Bachelier assumes arithmetic dynamics \(dF=\sigma_N\,dW\), which put no sign constraint on \(F\) or \(K\). Negative EUR, CHF and JPY forwards therefore forced the market from Black to normal quoting, not just a change of parameter.

front: Give the Bachelier call price for forward \(F\), strike \(K\), normal vol \(\sigma_N\) and expiry \(T\) (undiscounted), and derive the ATM value.
back:
With \(d=(F-K)/(\sigma_N\sqrt{T})\): \[C=(F-K)\,N(d)+\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\,\varphi(d)\] At \(F=K\), \(d=0\), so \(C=\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\,\varphi(0)=\sigma_N\sqrt{T}/\sqrt{2\pi}\approx 0.4\,\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\). Only the density term survives at the money because the intrinsic term vanishes.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the ATM straddle about \(0.8\,\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\)? The straddle payoff is \(|F_T-K|\), and for a centred Gaussian \(\mathbb E|X|=\sigma\sqrt{T}\sqrt{2/\pi}\approx 0.8\,\sigma\sqrt{T}\). Each leg is half that.

front: For an ATM option in the normal model, the premium per unit of \(\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\) is {{c1::0.4}} per leg (exact value \(1/\sqrt{2\pi}\)), and {{c2::0.8}} for a straddle.
back: Quick premium estimate: premium per leg \(\approx 0.4\,\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\), multiplied by the annuity for a swaption or by the discount factor for a cap.

front: Convert a 20% lognormal ATM vol on a 2% forward into an approximate normal vol in bp per year.
back:
First-order ATM rule: \(\sigma_N\approx\sigma_B F\). So \(0.20\times 0.02=0.004\), about 40bp per year normal.
Rule of thumb: normal vol \(\approx\) lognormal vol \(\times\) forward. This matches ATM prices to first order only. Away from the money, and for long expiries, the mapping depends on strike and on the smile.
Interviewer follow-up: If the rate doubles to 4% at constant 20% lognormal vol, the normal vol doubles to about 80bp. A book quoted in lognormal vol therefore has bp-vega that scales with the level of rates.

front: At the money, \(\sigma_N \approx \sigma_B \times\){{c1::forward rate}}. Away from the money the leading-order conversion is \(\sigma_N\approx\sigma_B\,(F-K)/\ln(F/K)\), which is close to \(\sigma_B\sqrt{FK}\) near the money.
back: The ATM relation is the first-order price match. The strike-dependent factor is a geometric-type mean of \(F\) and \(K\); it is smaller for low strikes, so the conversion depends on where on the smile you are.

front: A flat lognormal smile is quoted at a 2% forward. What does this imply for the normal smile, and why does it matter when comparing a Black quote with a normal quote?
back:
Using \(\sigma_N\approx\sigma_B\,(F-K)/\ln(F/K)\), the factor is smaller at low strikes, so a flat lognormal smile implies a normal smile that slopes upward in strike (lower normal vol at low strikes).
A "flat" Black smile is not flat in bp. Surfaces must be converted strike by strike before a Black quote is compared with a normal quote, or a fake skew appears.

front: What is the shifted-lognormal (displaced diffusion) model, and what is its main trade-off?
back:
Model \(F+s\) as lognormal: \(d(F+s)=\sigma_s\,(F+s)\,dW\), with shift \(s\) chosen so that \(F+s>0\) across the relevant range. Price with Black on \(F+s\) and \(K+s\).
It keeps Black's machinery and handles forwards below zero. Trade-offs: the shift is a free parameter fixed by convention; vols are only comparable at the same shift; and it still carries a lognormal-type skew rather than a true arithmetic one.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is a shifted vol not comparable across two different shifts? Because the lognormal vol is measured on \(F+s\), so the same bp move corresponds to a different percentage vol.

front: Why is normal (bp) vol the natural quoting unit when rates are near or below zero?
back:
(1) Lognormal vol is relative: \(\sigma_B=\sigma_N/F\). For a fixed bp move, lognormal vol explodes as \(F\to 0\) and is undefined for \(F\le 0\).
(2) Normal vol is an absolute bp-per-year measure, stable across rate levels.
(3) It matches Gaussian short-rate models (Vasicek, Hull-White) and the SABR \(\beta=0\) framework used in practice.
Normal quoting does not remove the smile. Normal markets still show skew, which is handled by \(\beta=0\) SABR or a shifted model.

front: Give delta, gamma and vega of a normal-model call in closed form, and their ATM values.
back:
With \(d\) as above: \[\Delta=N(d),\qquad \Gamma=\frac{\varphi(d)}{\sigma_N\sqrt{T}},\qquad \mathcal{V}=\sqrt{T}\,\varphi(d)\] At the money: \(\Delta=0.5\), \(\Gamma=\varphi(0)/(\sigma_N\sqrt{T})\approx 0.4/(\sigma_N\sqrt{T})\), \(\mathcal{V}\approx 0.4\sqrt{T}\).
Interviewer follow-up: Greeks depend on \(F\) and \(K\) only through \(d\), so for fixed \(\sigma_N\) and \(T\) the ATM gamma is the same at every rate level. This is why normal greeks are stated in bp.

front: A dealer quotes flat cap vols at 1y, 2y, 3y and so on. Explain how you strip forward caplet volatilities, and why flat vols cannot be used directly as caplet vols.
back:
A flat cap vol applies one vol to every caplet in the cap. The cap price is \(\text{Cap}(T_n)=\sum_{i\le n}\text{Cpl}_i(\sigma_i)\), a sum of forward-period caplets.
Bootstrap one period at a time: for each new maturity, solve for the single new caplet vol \(\sigma_n\) that reproduces the new flat cap price, holding earlier caplet vols fixed.
Flat vols mix caplets of different expiries, so they are a quoting convention, not the forward vol term structure. Stripped caplet vols can be unstable or non-monotone, so they are smoothed or interpolated before use.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the first caplet of a spot-starting cap not priced with vol? Its fixing is already set, so its value is deterministic.

front: State cap-floor parity at a common strike \(K\), and explain why it needs no volatility model.
back:
\[\text{Cap}(K)-\text{Floor}(K)=\sum_i N\tau_i P(0,T_i)\,\big(F_i-K\big)\] The right-hand side is the value of a forward-start payer swap at fixed rate \(K\). Each caplet minus floorlet equals \(\tau_i N P(0,T_i)\big[(F_i-K)^+-(K-F_i)^+\big]=\tau_i N P(0,T_i)(F_i-K)\), which is linear in the forward. No distribution is assumed, so parity holds for any model and any smile.
Interviewer follow-up: At which strike do cap and floor have equal value? At the forward swap rate, where the payer swap is worth zero.

front: Cap(K) minus Floor(K) at the same strike equals a {{c1::payer swap}} at fixed rate K. At the at-the-money strike (the forward swap rate) its value is {{c2::zero}}, so cap and floor have equal premium.
back: Holds for any model. Used to check that quoted cap and floor vols are consistent across strikes and across the cap and floor quotes.

front: Why do caplets on compounded overnight rates (SONIA, SOFR) not price the same way as legacy term-rate caplets?
back:
The period rate is compounded from daily fixings, \(r_c=\frac{1}{\tau}\big(\prod_d(1+r_d\delta_d)-1\big)\). The payoff depends on the whole path of overnight rates across the period, not on one forward fixing known at the period start.
Standard practice: price compounded-in-arrears caplets from a forward compounded rate with a convexity or timing adjustment, or from a model of overnight rates. Calibrate vols to compounded-cap quotes; a term-rate vol surface is not directly reusable.
Interviewer follow-up: Which adjustment is needed for in-arrears fixings? A convexity adjustment, because the compounded rate is not a martingale under the payment measure.

front: Flat 1y cap vol is 60bp normal and flat 2y cap vol is 55bp normal. Where is the forward 1y-to-2y caplet normal vol relative to 55bp, and why?
back:
Bootstrap: the 1y caplet carries 60bp, which is more than 55bp, so it absorbs more of the 2y cap premium. The value left for the second caplet is smaller than a 55bp caplet would be worth, so its implied vol is below 55bp.
The forward caplet vol falls by more than the flat vol does, and can sit well below the flat 2y quote. This comes from the stripping logic, not from a fixed rule.
Interviewer follow-up: Practical consequence? Price and hedge non-standard exposures off caplet or forward vols, never off flat vols.

front: Write the payer swaption value using the annuity and a Black-type expression, and name the measure under which it is an expectation.
back:
With annuity \(A=\sum_i\tau_i P(0,T_i)\) and forward swap rate \(S=(P(0,T_0)-P(0,T_n))/A\): \[V_{\text{pay}}=A\,\mathbb{E}^{A}\big[(S_{T_0}-K)^+\big]=A\,\big[S\,N(d_1)-K\,N(d_2)\big]\] for the Black case. The expectation is under the annuity measure, with numeraire \(A(t)\), under which \(S\) is a martingale. The normal analogue is \(A\,[(S-K)N(d)+\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\varphi(d)]\).
Interviewer follow-up: Why is \(S\) driftless under the annuity measure but not under the spot measure? \(S\) is a ratio of bond prices, and dividing by the annuity removes the drift.

front: State payer-receiver parity for European swaptions, and say what it implies at the money.
back:
Payer minus receiver with the same expiry, tenor and strike \(K\) equals the forward-start swap value \(A\,(S-K)\), with no volatility input. At \(K=S\), payer and receiver premia are equal.
A discrepancy at the money usually signals inconsistent conventions (annuity, day count, strike definition) rather than a model error.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the delta of an ATM payer in rate units? The payer delta is \(A\,N(d)\), so at the money it is about \(0.5\,A\) per unit of rate.

front: For an ATM European swaption in the normal model, the premium per leg is approximately {{c1::0.4}} times \(\sigma_N\sqrt{T}\) times the annuity. A payer or receiver with 100bp normal vol, 1y expiry and annuity 4.6 costs about {{c2::1.8%}} of notional.
back: Working: \(0.4\times 0.01\times 1\times 4.6\approx 0.0184\). Approximate mental-math rule only; the exact value comes from the normal formula. The annuity 4.6 is an approximate value for a 5y annual swap at about 3%.

front: You buy a 1y x 5y ATM straddle, payer plus receiver. Describe its delta, gamma and vega, and when it is a clean volatility trade.
back:
At inception the payer delta (about \(+0.5A\)) and receiver delta (about \(-0.5A\)) cancel, so the straddle is approximately delta-neutral. It is long gamma and long vega, with vega of about \(0.8\sqrt{T}\,A\) in normal units.
Its P&L depends on realised rate moves against the implied normal vol, plus theta. It is a clean vol trade only while the forward stays near the strike. As the rate moves, delta builds up and must be hedged, and the wings remain exposed.

front: How do you build a full swaption vol surface (expiry × tenor × strike) from market quotes, and which no-arbitrage conditions must the interpolation preserve?
back:
Quotes: ATM normal vols on an expiry × tenor grid, plus strike spreads at standard offsets, in normal bp. Each slice is converted to strike vols with a smile model (typically SABR fitted per expiry and tenor).
Calendar (expiry) direction: interpolate total variance \(\sigma^2T\) rather than vol, at fixed strike. Total variance must not fall with expiry. Example: at a fixed strike, 1y normal vol 100bp and 2y normal vol 70bp give total variance \(1.00\times10^{-4}\) at 1y and \(0.98\times10^{-4}\) at 2y, which is calendar arbitrage.
Strike direction: each slice must give a non-negative density (butterfly \(\ge0\)) and monotone call prices.
Tenor direction: there is no separate arbitrage condition, but the forward swap rate and annuity for each tenor must come from one consistent curve. A mismatch is a data error.
Interviewer follow-up: Why interpolate variance and not vol? Linear interpolation of total variance between monotone knots stays monotone. Linear interpolation of vol can create a dip in total variance.

front: Why is bucketed-vega hedging with co-tenor swaptions only approximate, and what determines the residual? Use the 1y×10y payer versus 1y×5y ratio as the first number.
back:
Bucketed vega is matched to first order in the normal vol of each bucket at inception. The residual has four sources.
(1) Mapping error. The split of vega across buckets comes from the risk system's key-rate or PCA mapping. A different mapping gives a different hedge.
(2) Strike mismatch. Off-ATM vega is \(\sqrt T\varphi(d)\) with \(d\ne0\), so a hedge at a different strike has different vega per unit notional.
(3) Vol-surface shape. Bucket vols do not move in parallel. Two hedges control two directions, not the full surface.
(4) Second-order terms. Volga and vanna are not matched by first-order vega.
Number: ATM vega per unit notional is proportional to \(A\sqrt T\). A 1y×10y (annuity about 8.53) carries about 1.86 times the vega per notional of a 1y×5y (annuity about 4.58). Hedging 100mm of 1y×10y therefore needs about 186mm of 1y×5y, before any bucket mapping.
Interviewer follow-up: Why not hedge with the same instrument? The point is the desk does not carry the 1y×10y; the hedge is chosen for liquidity and bucket coverage.

front: A payer and a receiver with the same expiry, tenor and strike show different implied normal vols in your system. Give the checks, in order, before you touch the smile model.
back:
1. Forward and annuity. Both legs must use one forward swap rate and one annuity: the same curve, the same discounting (OIS versus IBOR), the same day count and the same payment schedule.
2. Strike definition. The strike must be one number in both. Check the day count, compounding and any spread or shift.
3. Settlement. Cash versus physical settlement changes the annuity used for the premium.
4. Quote timing. A payer and receiver quoted at different times on a moving market are not comparable. Check that the quotes are simultaneous.
A consistent model gives identical implied vols for payer and receiver with the same strike, by payer-receiver parity. Only after these checks is a smile mismatch a model question.

front: In SABR, \(\alpha\) sets the {{c1::level}} of volatility, \(\beta\) is the {{c2::CEV exponent}} (0 normal, 1 lognormal), \(\rho\) is the {{c3::spot-vol correlation}} that drives skew, and \(\nu\) is the {{c4::vol-of-vol}} that drives curvature.
back: Dynamics: \(dF=\alpha F^{\beta}\,dW_1\), \(d\alpha=\nu\alpha\,dW_2\), with \(\langle dW_1,dW_2\rangle=\rho\,dt\).

front: What is the SABR backbone, and how does \(\beta\) control it?
back:
The backbone is how ATM vol moves as the forward moves. In lognormal terms \(\sigma_{\text{ATM}}\approx\alpha F^{\beta-1}\). Equivalently, normal ATM vol is \(\approx\alpha F^{\beta}\).
\(\beta=0\): normal ATM vol is constant in \(F\), so ATM vol does not respond to the rate level. \(\beta=1\): ATM lognormal vol is constant, so normal vol is proportional to \(F\).
Interviewer follow-up: Why do desks fix \(\beta\) rather than fit it? A smile alone barely identifies \(\beta\), so it is set by convention or by historical regression of ATM vol against the rate.

front: What is Hagan's SABR formula, and why is it an approximation rather than an exact price?
back:
Hagan et al. (2002) give an implied-vol formula from an asymptotic expansion in the expiry, with a near-ATM expansion in \(\ln(F/K)\). The price is then the Black or Bachelier formula evaluated at that implied vol. It is a closed-form smile, not an exact solution of the SDE.
It is accurate for short to moderate expiries and moderate strikes. Errors grow for long expiries, large \(\nu\) and far wings.
Interviewer follow-up: What is its main failure? The implied density can go negative at low strikes, which is static arbitrage.

front: How can Hagan-implied SABR smiles admit static arbitrage, and how do you detect it?
back:
Under a smile, the risk-neutral density is the discounted second derivative of the call with respect to strike (Breeden-Litzenberger). The Hagan expansion does not guarantee \(\partial_K^2 C\ge 0\). For large \(\nu\), long expiries, or low strikes with \(\beta=0\), the density can go negative.
Detection: price calls on a strike grid from the implied vols, then test the butterfly \(C(K-h)-2C(K)+C(K+h)\ge 0\) and the monotonicity \(\partial_K C\le 0\).
Interviewer follow-up: Fixes? Use a no-arbitrage variant such as Doust's free-boundary SABR, or enforce the density check inside calibration.

front: The risk-neutral density implied by a call price curve is the discounted {{c1::second derivative of the call price with respect to strike}}, which must be non-negative for the smile to be arbitrage-free.
back: Breeden-Litzenberger. In the Hagan expansion this is not automatic, so it has to be checked numerically on a strike grid.

front: Compare free-boundary SABR and ZABR as responses to the limitations of Hagan's SABR.
back:
Free-boundary SABR (Antonov, Konikov and Spector, Risk 2015) lets the forward move below zero through a free boundary, so no shift is needed. It has an exact price at zero correlation and a one-dimensional integral approximation otherwise. Its arbitrage-freeness is not guaranteed in general, which the same authors later address with a mixed model.
No-arbitrage SABR (Doust, 2012) instead puts an absorbing boundary at zero and writes the density as a sum of positive components, with prices by numerical integration. It targets the same low-strike density problem by a different route.
ZABR (Andreasen and Huge) generalises the volatility dynamics to \(d\sigma\propto\sigma^{\gamma}\). The volatility exponent controls the vol-of-vol shape separately, which improves long-expiry smiles and wing behaviour.
All three trade some simplicity for better wing behaviour and no-arbitrage properties.

front: What do \(\rho\) and \(\nu\) control in the SABR smile, and why is this separation useful in calibration?
back:
\( ho\) controls skew: negative \( ho\) makes implied vol rise as strike falls. \( u\) controls curvature and wing growth. To leading order skew scales with \( ho\) and curvature with \( u^2\).
The separation lets the risk reversal be matched by \( ho\) and the butterfly by \( u\), so each expiry-tenor slice is close to a two-dimensional problem rather than a tangled one.
Interviewer follow-up: If \( u o 0\), what remains? Only the CEV-induced skew, with no curvature from vol-of-vol.

front: Why is \(\beta=0\) (normal SABR) the usual choice when rates are low or negative, and what does it give up?
back:
\(\beta=0\) makes the forward process arithmetic, \(dF=\alpha\,dW\). This has no positivity constraint and matches normal quoting.
Trade-offs: the normal ATM vol is flat in \(F\), so it does not respond to the rate level. Its wing behaviour is also the source of the low-strike negative density issue, and \(\beta\) still has to be chosen by convention or regression.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is \(\beta=1\) a poor fit at low rates? Lognormal dynamics force vol to blow up as \(F\to 0\), which conflicts with normal-quoted markets.

front: When the forward turns negative during a SABR calibration, what must change in the set-up?
back: The lognormal Hagan formula is undefined once \(F\le 0\) or \(K\le 0\). Options are: calibrate \(\beta=0\) in the normal Hagan expansion; use a shifted SABR with a shift large enough that \(F+s>0\) on the grid; or switch to free-boundary SABR. The calibration grid must then include strikes below zero, and the fit should be done on normal vols so that the strikes are comparable.

front: Two SABR calibrations fit today's smile equally well but give different deltas. Why?
back:
Static fit does not pin the dynamics. How the smile moves when the forward moves is set by \(\beta\) and \(\rho\), and by the backbone. Those change the smile-adjusted delta \(\partial V/\partial F\) even when the static smile matches.
This is the sticky-strike versus sticky-delta question, and it sets the hedge ratio.

front: Distinguish sticky-strike and sticky-delta smile dynamics, and give the smile-adjusted delta formula.
back:
Sticky strike: the implied vol at each fixed strike is unchanged when the forward moves, so \(\partial\sigma/\partial F=0\).
Sticky delta: the vol at a fixed moneyness \(K/F\) is unchanged, so the smile shifts with the forward.
\[\Delta_{\text{smile}}=\frac{\partial V}{\partial F}=\Delta_{\text{BS}}+\mathcal{V}\,\frac{\partial\sigma(K,F)}{\partial F}\] Sticky strike gives \(\Delta_{\text{smile}}=\Delta_{\text{BS}}\). Under sticky delta the second term is non-zero and is typically large for a skewed smile.
Interviewer follow-up: Which is right? Neither by default. It is an empirical choice, often checked by regressing vol moves against rate moves, and it determines the hedge ratio.

front: Derive vanna and volga for a normal-model call, and show that both vanish at the money.
back:
With \(\Delta=N(d)\), \(\mathcal{V}=\sqrt{T}\varphi(d)\), \(\partial_\sigma d=-d/\sigma\):
Vanna \(=\partial_\sigma\Delta=\varphi(d)\,\partial_\sigma d=-\dfrac{d\,\varphi(d)}{\sigma}\)
Volga \(=\partial_\sigma\mathcal{V}=\sqrt{T}\,\varphi'(d)\,\partial_\sigma d=\dfrac{\sqrt{T}\,d^2\varphi(d)}{\sigma}\)
Both are zero at \(d=0\). Vanna is odd in \(d\), so it measures skew sensitivity. Volga is non-negative and grows with \(d^2\), so it lives in the wings.
Interviewer follow-up: What does this mean for hedging? ATM options carry no volga, so volga hedges must be placed in the wings.

front: In the normal model with zero drift, vega equals \({{c1::\sigma_N T\,\Gamma}}\) at every strike, so theta equals \({{c2::-\sigma_N\,\mathcal V/(2T)}}\).
back: Derivation: \(\Theta=-\tfrac12\sigma_N^2\Gamma\), and \(\Gamma=\mathcal V/(\sigma_NT)\). See the derivation card on the vega and theta relations.

front: Show that the normal (Bachelier) price satisfies \(\partial_t V+\tfrac12\sigma_N^2\,\partial_{FF}V=0\), and derive the gamma-theta relation.
back:
Under \(dF=\sigma_N\,dW\), Itô gives \(dV=\partial_tV\,dt+\partial_FV\,dF+\tfrac12\sigma_N^2\partial_{FF}V\,dt\). Since \(V\) is a martingale under the forward measure, the drift term must vanish, so \(\partial_tV=-\tfrac12\sigma_N^2\Gamma\).
Theta is therefore exactly the negative of expected gamma P&L at the implied variance. A long-gamma position pays theta in proportion to gamma and variance. Discounting or a non-zero drift adds a rate term.
Interviewer follow-up: Compare with Black: \(\Theta=-\tfrac12\sigma_B^2F^2\Gamma\).

front: Derive the expected delta-hedged P&L of a long normal-model option, and explain why it depends on realised versus implied vol.
back:
Delta-hedge with \(\Delta\). The position's P&L over a small step is \(\tfrac12\Gamma\,(dF)^2+\Theta\,dt\). Using \(\Theta=-\tfrac12\sigma_i^2\Gamma\) and realised variance in place of \((dF)^2\): \[\text{P\&L}\approx\tfrac12\,\Gamma\,\big(\sigma_r^2-\sigma_i^2\big)\,dt\] Over the life, \(\tfrac12\Gamma T(\sigma_r^2-\sigma_i^2)\). The long gamma position profits when realised exceeds implied.
Interviewer follow-up: ATM 1y option, \(\sigma_i=80\)bp, \(\sigma_r=100\)bp. Gamma is about \(0.4/0.008\approx 50\) per unit rate. P&L \(\approx\tfrac12\times 50\times(0.01^2-0.008^2)\approx 9\times 10^{-4}\), about 9bp of notional.

front: Explain vol-of-vol and correlation risk in a CMS spread option, and state the sign of a long spread-call position's exposure to correlation.
back:
Vol-of-vol (\(\nu\) in SABR) changes the wings of each underlying's smile, which changes the tails of the spread distribution.
Correlation: the spread \(S_1-S_2\) has variance \(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2-2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\). Higher correlation reduces dispersion, so a long spread call loses value as \(\rho\) rises. The holder is short correlation. A long straddle on the spread is a dispersion bet and has the same sign.
Correlation is rarely traded directly, so this is a model risk to hedge with related options or bound with scenarios.

front: In HJM under the risk-neutral measure, with \(df(t,T)=\alpha\,dt+\sigma(t,T)\,dW_t\), what is the forward-rate drift \(\alpha\)?
back:
\[\alpha(t,T)=\sigma(t,T)\int_t^T\sigma(t,u)\,du\] Derivation: the bond price is \(P(t,T)=\exp(-\int_t^T f(t,u)\,du)\). Requiring discounted bond prices to be martingales forces the forward drift to be the volatility times the integral of the volatilities.
Interviewer follow-up: What does this imply about freedom in the model? The drift is fully determined by the volatilities, so the model is specified by \(\sigma(t,T)\) alone.

front: Why does Hull-White 1F sit inside HJM, and what volatility function does it imply?
back:
Hull-White, \(dr=(\theta(t)-a r)\,dt+\sigma\,dW\), is an HJM model with deterministic, separable volatility \(\sigma(t,T)=\sigma e^{-a(T-t)}\). Substituting this into the HJM drift gives a Markov short rate with the correct no-arbitrage drift.
The exponential decay in \(T-t\) is what makes the model Markovian with a single factor, and it generates mean reversion.
Interviewer follow-up: Exact bond price? \(P(t,T)=A(t,T)\,e^{-B(t,T)r_t}\) with \(B(t,T)=(1-e^{-a(T-t)})/a\).

front: In Hull-White 1F, \(P(t,T)=A(t,T)\exp(-B\,r_t)\) with \(B(t,T)=\){{c1::(1-e^{-a(T-t)})/a}}. Starting from \(r_0\) with constant \(\sigma\), the variance of \(r_t\) is {{c2::\(\sigma^2(1-e^{-2at})/(2a)\)}}.
back: Second result is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck variance. Mean reversion caps the variance as \(t\) grows.

front: In one-factor Hull-White, what does the mean-reversion parameter \(a\) change in the swap-rate vol term structure, and why do forward-rate moves stay perfectly correlated?
back:
All instantaneous forward moves load on the same \(dW\) with \(\sigma e^{-a(T-t)}\). Any two forward rates or swap rates are therefore perfectly correlated in a one-factor model. Mean reversion does not decorrelate them.
What \(a\) changes is the relative loading of each swap rate on the short rate. The swap-rate vol is \(\sigma|\partial_rS|\). For a 1y×5y swap on a flat 3% curve, \(|\partial_rS|\) is 0.930 at \(a=0.03\) and 0.738 at \(a=0.10\). For the same 100bp swap vol, the short-rate vol must be about 1.07% at \(a=0.03\) and about 1.35% at \(a=0.10\).
Decorrelation needs a second factor, as in a two-factor Hull-White model with a correlation parameter.
Interviewer follow-up: So what does calibration identify? The co-terminal vols identify \(\sigma(t)\) given \(a\), and the mix of short and long tenor vols constrains \(a\) only weakly.

front: Describe calibrating Hull-White 1F to a swaption surface, and name the main limitation.
back:
Step 1: fit the time-dependent drift \(\theta(t)\) so the model reproduces today's discount curve exactly.
Step 2: fit the piecewise-constant \(\sigma(t)\) and \(a\) so that model swaption prices match the target expiry-by-tenor vols, weighting the most liquid points. Prices come from Jamshidian's decomposition into zero-coupon bond options, or from a tree.
Limitation: one Gaussian factor gives a single correlation structure, and the smile is missing. The fit is good at the money and poor in the wings.
Interviewer follow-up: What is Jamshidian's trick? It splits a European swaption into a portfolio of zero-coupon bond options, struck so that each leg is exercised consistently, which gives a fast price in one-factor models.

front: How is a Bermudan swaption priced in a one-factor Hull-White model, and what decision is made on each exercise date?
back:
Build a trinomial tree (or solve a PDE) for the short rate, with nodes spanning all time steps to the last exercise date.
At each exercise date \(t_k\), node value \(=\max(\text{exercise value},\text{continuation value})\). Exercise value is the PV of the remaining swap at that node. Continuation value is the discounted expected value one step later.
Backward induction gives the price at inception. The tree must be calibrated to the discount curve and the swaption surface, otherwise the Bermudan premium carries a wrong vol level even if the algorithm is correct.

front: What is the Bermudan exercise boundary, and why is a Bermudan worth at least as much as its best European component?
back:
The exercise boundary is the set of state values (swap rate or short rate) at each date where exercise and continuation values are equal. Exercise is optimal beyond it. It is a time-dependent threshold, found by backward induction.
A Bermudan can choose its exercise date, and each European option is one of its choices. So the Bermudan is at least the maximum of the European swaptions, and the difference is the value of early-exercise optionality.
Interviewer follow-up: For a payer Bermudan, which region of the state variable triggers exercise? The high-rate region.

front: How would you price a Bermudan when the model is multi-factor or not tree-friendly, such as an LMM?
back:
Use Monte Carlo with Longstaff-Schwartz regression. Simulate paths. At each exercise date, regress discounted future cashflows of continuing paths on basis functions of the state (for example swap rates) to estimate continuation value. Exercise where intrinsic value exceeds the estimate, and roll back.
The regression policy is sub-optimal, so the price is a lower bound. An upper bound comes from dual methods (Andersen-Broadie). Trade-offs: basis choice, path count, and harder Greeks, which need pathwise or AAD methods.

front: In the lognormal forward-rate model (BGM/LMM), what is the drift of \(L_i\) under the terminal measure \(\mathbb{Q}^{T_N}\)?
back:
Under \(dL_i=\sigma_i L_i\,dW_i\) with \(\langle dW_i,dW_j\rangle=\rho_{ij}\,dt\), a change of numeraire from \(T_i\) to \(T_N\) gives \[dL_i=-\sigma_i L_i\sum_{j=i+1}^{N}\frac{\tau_j\,\rho_{ij}\,\sigma_j L_j}{1+\tau_j L_j}\,dt+\sigma_i L_i\,dW_i^{T_N}\] The drift is a finite sum over later rates, with a negative sign. It comes from the change of numeraire to the bond maturing at \(T_N\).
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the terminal measure convenient but not always used? It needs one drift sum and one numeraire, but simulating to \(T_N\) is a long path. Bermudan pricing often uses the spot-LIBOR measure instead.

front: How is an LMM calibrated to caplets and swaptions, and what does the correlation matrix do?
back:
Caplets: each \(L_i\) has a Black caplet, so \(\int_0^{T_{i-1}}\sigma_i(t)^2\,dt\) is fixed by the caplet vol. This pins the time-dependent volatility of each rate.
Swaptions: approximate the swaption vol from the \(\sigma_i\) and the correlation (for example Rebonato's frozen-weights approximation), then fit the correlation to swaption prices.
Correlation is the remaining degree of freedom. The market constrains only part of it, so parametric forms such as exponential decay are used, and this choice matters for Bermudans.

front: What is rank reduction in an LMM, and why does it matter for pricing?
back:
The correlation matrix is \(N\times N\) and must be positive semi-definite. Rank reduction writes each correlation as an inner product of unit-norm vectors in \(d\) dimensions, for example Rebonato's parametrisation, or a PCA of the correlation.
A small number of factors, often 2 or 3, captures most of the variance of rate moves. This speeds simulation at the cost of approximation error in the correlation, which can shift the swaption fit and Bermudan value.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the trade-off? Fewer factors lose correlation fidelity. More factors slow simulation and overfit.

front: Two LMM calibrations fit the same swaption cube but price a Bermudan very differently. What is the likely cause, and how would you check it?
back:
The swaption cube constrains only part of the correlation matrix. The Bermudan depends on how forward rates decorrelate across tenors and on the smile dynamics. Different correlation parametrisations or rank-reduction choices can fit the vanilla surface yet imply different forward correlations, which change the Bermudan's exercise value.
Check: compare implied forward correlations with a historical PCA of rate changes, and measure the Bermudan's sensitivity to the correlation parametrisation.

front: Why does a one-factor Gaussian model with constant \(\sigma\) miss the smile across strikes, and what does a local-vol leverage function fix that a stochastic-vol component does not?
back:
With constant \(\sigma\), the normal model has no state dependence in its vol, so the smile has no dynamic skew. Cheyette and SLV add state dependence. In an SLV, the leverage function \(L(t,S)\) multiplies a stochastic-vol component, so \(\sigma_{\rm loc}=L\cdot\sigma_{\rm stoch}\).
The leverage function is calibrated so the model reproduces today's vanilla marginals exactly. The stochastic component controls how the smile moves through time, which is what exotic values depend on.
Interviewer follow-up: Why can a model with an exact vanilla fit still misprice a forward-starting option? Matching today's surface fixes only the marginals at today's date. A forward smile depends on the stochastic component, which is not pinned by the vanilla quotes.

front: Why is a CMS rate not equal to the forward swap rate, and what sign does the convexity adjustment usually have for a payer CMS?
back:
A CMS coupon fixes the swap rate \(S(T_f)\) at \(T_f\) and pays at a later date \(T_p\). The forward swap rate is a martingale under the annuity measure, but the payment at \(T_p\) needs the \(T_p\)-forward measure, under which \(S\) has a drift.
The convexity adjustment \(\mathbb{E}^{T_p}[S]-S_0\) is positive for a payment after fixing, so the CMS rate is above the forward swap rate. Its size grows with \(\sigma^2 T_f\) and with the payment lag \(T_p-T_f\).
Interviewer follow-up: What happens to the adjustment as the lag shrinks to zero? It tends to zero, and the CMS rate tends to the forward swap rate.

front: Give the static replication formula for \(\mathbb{E}^{A}[g(S)]\) and explain how it prices CMS-type payoffs with a full smile.
back:
Decompose \(g\) around the forward \(F_0\): \(g(S)=g(F_0)+\int_{-\infty}^{F_0}g''(K)(K-S)^+\,dK+\int_{F_0}^{\infty}g''(K)(S-K)^+\,dK\). Taking expectations under the annuity measure: \[\mathbb{E}^{A}[g(S)]=g(F_0)+\int_{-\infty}^{F_0}g''(K)\,\mathrm{Rec}(K)\,dK+\int_{F_0}^{\infty}g''(K)\,\mathrm{Pay}(K)\,dK\] where \(\mathrm{Pay}(K)\) and \(\mathrm{Rec}(K)\) are the payer and receiver swaption prices per unit annuity, taken from the market smile at each strike. Rates can be negative, so the lower limit is \(-\infty\), not 0. For a payment lag, a measure change is added.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is this better than a single-vol convexity formula? It uses the whole smile, so it captures wing and skew effects that a single vol misses.

front: For a CMS spread call on \(S_1-S_2\), the spread variance is \(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2-2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2\). Higher correlation {{c1::lowers}} the value of the call, so a long spread call is {{c2::short}} correlation.
back: Correlation between swap rates is rarely directly observable. It is typically inferred from the spread-option market or from history, with sensitivity checked across the plausible range.

front: How are CMS spread options priced with a copula, and what are the modelling assumptions?
back:
Price each swap rate's marginal distribution from its own smile model (for example SABR), under the consistent measure. Join the two marginals with a copula that has correlation \(\rho\). Then Monte Carlo or numerical integration gives \(\mathbb{E}[(S_1-S_2-K)^+]\).
Assumptions: the marginals are right, and the copula captures the joint law. A Gaussian copula has zero tail dependence, while a Student-t copula adds tail dependence, which changes joint extreme scenarios. Those extremes drive the value of spread options.
Interviewer follow-up: What does the choice of copula change for a spread option? Its joint tail behaviour, which matters for the spread's wings.

front: A {{c1::Gaussian}} copula has zero tail dependence. A Student-t copula with finite degrees of freedom has {{c2::positive}} tail dependence.
back: Relevant for CMS spread and other joint-extreme payoffs, where the choice of copula changes the value of the wings.

front: A range accrual pays a daily coupon when the 10y swap rate lies between 2% and 4%. The forward is 3%. Describe the investor's exposure, and estimate how often the note accrues if the normal vol over the period is 80bp for a one-period view at expiry.
back:
The coupon is \(\sum_d c\,\tau_d\,\mathbf 1\{L Vega: the in-range probability falls as vol rises, so the investor is short vol. Delta: near zero at the centre of the range by symmetry, and it grows as the rate approaches a boundary.
Number: with \(\sigma\sqrt T=0.8\%\), the boundaries are \(\pm1\%\) from the forward, so \(z=1.25\). The Gaussian in-range probability is \(1-2(1-N(1.25))=1-2(0.1056)\approx 79\%\) at expiry. This is a single-date approximation: the daily accrual is the average over the path.
Interviewer follow-up: If the reference is a CMS rate, what else matters? Correlation and the smile, because the in-range probability depends on the tail shape of the swap rate.

front: Describe the embedded option in a TARN (target redemption note), and say why the investor is short it without assuming which way the coupons move with rates.
back:
A TARN redeems when cumulative coupons reach a target. The redemption is a knockout on the coupon stream: once the target is hit, the investor gives up all future coupons.
The investor holds the coupons and is therefore short this knockout. Whether a rate path hits the target fast or slow depends on the coupon's dependence on rates. Either way, a path that hits the target early removes the coupons the investor would have kept.
Number: with a 6% target, an average coupon of 2.5% knocks out after about 2.4 years, and an average of 1% after 6 years. The time to knockout is about target divided by average coupon.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a single-vol model misprice it? The knockout depends on the whole coupon path, so the vol at each coupon date, the smile and the correlation between coupon dates all matter.

front: How does a callable structure relate to a Bermudan swaption, and which party is long or short vol?
back:
A callable bond is a non-callable bond plus or minus a Bermudan option on the rate, depending on which party holds the call. The call right belongs to the issuer, so the issuer is long a Bermudan option and long vol, while the investor is short that option and short vol.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a callable's price fall when vol rises? Higher vol raises the value of the issuer's call, which the investor has sold.

front: Two dealers quote the same swaption smile. One fits a normal SABR with \(\beta=0\), the other a shifted lognormal SABR. Why might their hedges still disagree even though both fit the vanilla surface?
back:
Both fit the static smile, but they differ in dynamics, which is what the hedge depends on. Their backbones differ, since \(\beta=0\) gives a flat normal ATM vol while a shifted lognormal backbone scales with \(F+s\). Their smile-adjusted deltas therefore differ.
The fix is to choose the model whose smile dynamics match the market's observed behaviour (regression of ATM vol on rates), not the one that fits today's surface best.
